title: Shackleton's Ship Was Trapped in Ice for 281 Days. How Did All 28 Men Come Back Alive?
description:
"Men wanted for hazardous journey. Small wages, constant danger." This is said to be Shackleton's recruiting ad, but no one has ever found the original, and it is generally regarded as a legend. Shackleton's own book says only that he "received nearly five thousand applications" after announcing the expedition, and Captain Worsley walked in after dreaming of a London street packed with ice blocks and then seeing a sign on a door-post. This episode covers only what the records hold: anchor weighed on December 5, 1914; on January 19, 1915, the ship was beset by ice in the Weddell Sea, held for 281 days while drifting more than 1,000 km, crushed in late October and sunk on November 21; the 28 men spent over five months on floating ice, then reached Elephant Island by small boat in under a week; Shackleton and five others sailed the James Caird about 1,300 km (he wrote 800 miles), and Worsley got only four sights of the sun the whole way; three men walked 36 hours straight across South Georgia; on the fourth rescue attempt, on August 30, 1916, everyone on the island was taken aboard. Last comes the wreck, found on March 5, 2022, 3,008 meters down.

"All came back alive" means the 28 men of the Endurance party; in the same expedition, three men of the other party, in the Ross Sea, did not return. Distances are converted from the latitudes and longitudes Shackleton himself gave (his miles are nautical miles). "The first landing ever made on Elephant Island" and "no one had gone more than a mile inland on South Georgia" are Shackleton's own claims in his book; that crossing is now called "the first recorded crossing." Shackleton recorded Frank Wild's reply at the rescue as "We are all well, boss," while a crew member's diary has "All safe, all well"; both are given. Sources for every quote, year and number are listed in the references below; a few items rest only on Wikipedia and are secondhand (over a year and four months without seeing land, 120 glass plates, the wreck about 10 km from the recorded position, the ship's original name Polaris). Sentences that begin "We think" are this channel's view.

The illustrations in this episode are AI-generated. Historical figures are drawn as cartoon characters, unnamed and not meant as likenesses; modern researchers are not drawn.

Information as of 2026-10-19 (rewritten on 2026-10-25 under new guidelines)

chapters.photographer: Gold dropped, photos kept; the wreck's position logged

e101.text: You've surely heard this ad: Men wanted for hazardous journey. Small wages, constant danger.

e102.text: Supposedly it drew 28 men, later locked in Antarctic ice almost 2 years.

e103.text: Early 1914, London. A captain dreamed a street was full of ice blocks and he sailed a ship through it.

e104.text: Later he passed a door whose sign read: Imperial Trans-Antarctic Expedition. Inside, Shackleton said: You're hired.

e105.text: This captain didn't come for an ad. So what page of Shackleton's own book has the ad?

e106.text: Later, six men took a small boat to find an island, guided only by the sun.

e107.text: Over a century later, an icebreaker went back to find it.

e108.text: This file follows their own diaries and logbooks through all 634 days.

e109.text: In the end, how many of them came back?

e201.text: Not one page. He wrote only that announcing the expedition brought nearly 5,000 applications.

e202.text: From these he picked 56 men, split into two equal parties; one party's ship was Endurance.

e203.text: Choosing from 5,000 letters, who would you pick?

e220.text: One man they clearly didn't pick ended up on the ship anyway.

e204.text: In Buenos Aires, a young man asked for work. Would they take him?

e205.text: Worsley, the opening's captain, wrote: they refused him; crew was full and he was too young.

e206.text: But at sea, he came out of hiding on his own; he'd been there two days with almost no food or drink.

e207.text: Worsley brought him to Shackleton and argued for keeping him.

e208.text: I couldn't help laughing here: the captain who just sent him away now speaks for him. And Shackleton?

e209.text: Shackleton took him on. He was Blackborow, 18 or 19, the youngest sailor aboard.

e210.text: Morning, December 5, 1914: Endurance weighed anchor at South Georgia.

e211.text: Shackleton wrote: the windlass's clank broke their last link with civilization.

e212.text: When would they next set foot on land?

e213.text: January 19, 1915, in the Weddell Sea: overnight, the ice closed around the ship.

e214.text: The next day, the ship was stuck fast. How long would it be held?

e216.text: All that time it kept moving: the ice carried it northwest over 1,000 kilometers.

e217.text: Late October, below minus 20 Celsius, the ice crushed the ship.

e218.text: At 5 p.m., Shackleton gave the order: all hands onto the ice.

e219.text: Then a man on the ice, facing the breaking ship, kept turning a handle. What was he doing?

e301.text: Filming. It was the photographer Hurley, shooting Endurance's last moments.

e302.text: The crow's nest crashed down 3 meters from him, and his camera never stopped.

e303.text: But marching on ice meant shedding things. Shackleton allowed each man 2 pounds of personal items, under a kilo.

e304.text: Gold coins were thrown away, photos were kept. I've reread that sentence many times.

e305.text: Of the Bible the Queen gave the ship, Shackleton took only the flyleaf.

e306.text: Hurley kept just 120 of his glass plates, and smashed all the rest.

e307.text: If you could keep only 120 of your life's best photos, how would you choose?

e308.text: The dogs, and the carpenter's cat, were later all shot.

e309.text: They made Ocean Camp on a floe over 2 kilometers away. The ship was still afloat. For how long?

e310.text: A crewman's diary: the evening of November 21, lying in the tents, they heard Shackleton shout: She's going!

e311.text: Bow down, stern in the air, she slid under in an instant; the ice closed over her.

e313.text: Keep that log entry in mind; it comes back at the end.

e314.text: Ship gone, where now? Shackleton reckoned the nearest spot with possible food and shelter was Paulet Island.

e315.text: There stood a Swedish expedition's hut, stocked with food but uninhabited.

e316.text: Distance: about 640 kilometers. Could people standing on drifting ice walk that far?

e317.text: They later moved to another floe, Patience Camp, for nearly three and a half months.

e318.text: Never reaching Paulet Island, they drifted on ice nearly five and a half months.

e319.text: April 9, 1916, 1 p.m.: they had to leave the floe and push their three boats into the water.

e320.text: The three boats were named after donors; one of them was the James Caird.

e321.text: Three small boats rowed out into open sea.

e401.text: Whatever the route, nights came first: early on they hauled boats onto floes overnight, back in at dawn.

e402.text: In under a week, April 15, they reached Elephant Island.

e403.text: Earlier I asked: when would they next set foot on land? Answer: over a year and four months after leaving South Georgia.

e415.text: Shackleton wrote: the island's first-ever landing, the honor due to the youngest.

e405.text: The first he told to jump was the stowaway boy, Blackborow.

e406.text: Feet already frostbitten, he sat down hard; Shackleton said he was the first to 'sit' on the island.

e407.text: Others landed, scooped up pebbles, and let them trickle through their fingers.

e408.text: Reading this, I felt I was holding stones too.

e409.text: But there was no one else here.

e410.text: If you were Shackleton, on this stony beach, what would you do next?

e411.text: They flipped two boats over to use as roofs.

e412.text: Shackleton's plan: the third, James Caird, goes to South Georgia for help.

e413.text: To South Georgia, Shackleton wrote: 800 miles, about 1,300 kilometers.

e414.text: This is just crazy: six men in one small open wooden boat.

e501.text: On the morning of April 24, Shackleton set out with five men; Worsley navigated.

e502.text: Frank Wild led the 22 left on the island.

e503.text: Of 24 chronometers at the start, only one still ran; their position hung on Worsley seeing the sun.

e504.text: For a sextant sight, he knelt on a thwart, a sailor holding him on each side.

e505.text: Yet for six full days after setting out, he didn't get a single sight.

e506.text: Remember 'guided only by the sun' from the start? All voyage long, he sighted the sun just four times.

e507.text: In that boat, your navigator seeing the sun only every few days, would you panic?

e508.text: Worsley himself wrote that it made him very uneasy.

e509.text: Worse was coming. On day 11, Shackleton saw white on the horizon and thought the clouds had parted.

e510.text: It wasn't cloud but the crest of a giant wave. In 26 years at sea, he'd never seen one so big.

e512.text: Every time I read this, I hold my breath.

e513.text: Day 14, May 8: someone spotted the black cliffs of South Georgia.

e514.text: But a storm kept them at sea two more days. On day 16, the evening of May 10, they landed at King Haakon Bay.

e515.text: Problem: the whaling station was on the island's far side.

e516.text: Remember the 1,300 kilometers? Behind them now. Just about 31 kilometers, straight line, to the station.

e517.text: In between: nameless mountains and glaciers.

e518.text: Shackleton wrote: none had ever gone over a mile inland.

e519.text: Could they cross mountains no one had walked?

e601.text: May 19, 2 a.m.: Shackleton, Worsley and Crean ate a hot meal and set off; three others stayed on the beach.

e602.text: Over mountains and glaciers, they walked 36 hours straight.

e603.text: Today it's called the first recorded crossing of South Georgia's interior.

e604.text: At last, they walked into Stromness whaling station.

e605.text: The manager looked at the three and said, hesitantly: I know your voice... You're the mate of the Daisy?

e608.text: The manager told him: The war is not over. Millions are being killed. Europe is mad. The world is mad.

e609.text: When they left, that great war had only just begun. Reading this, I froze for a second.

e610.text: The island party still waited under the boats.

e701.text: From May to July, Shackleton tried three times. First, a steamer was stopped by ice 70 miles from Elephant Island.

e702.text: Second, a trawler got within 32 kilometers before ice drove it back; third, a sailing ship failed too.

e703.text: The ice held. By the third failure, I was really worried for the island party. Would they last?

e704.text: On August 25, Shackleton set out a fourth time, in a small Chilean steel steamer, the Yelcho.

e705.text: He had promised: the ship would never touch ice.

e706.text: Would the ice part this time?

e707.text: The morning of August 30, 1916, Worsley spotted the island camp first.

e708.text: Shackleton shouted ashore: Are you all well? If you were ashore, what would you shout?

e709.text: Wild replied: We are all well, boss. Then three cheers rang out from the shore.

e710.text: A crewman's diary on the island recorded it differently: All safe, all well.

e711.text: Within an hour, everyone was aboard. Four and a half months in, their food was nearly gone.

e712.text: The opening question: how many came back? All 28 on Endurance came back alive.

e713.text: From the day they weighed anchor: 634 days. Shackleton himself said nearly two years.

e714.text: But 'all' means only Endurance. The other party?

e715.text: In the Ross Sea, across Antarctica, three never came back.

e716.text: Two were lost on the same date the James Caird sighted South Georgia.

e717.text: And the ship under the ice? Could it be found?

e801.text: It could. In March 2022, a South African icebreaker sailed into the Weddell Sea.

e802.text: That icebreaker from the opening found Endurance on March 5, 3,008 meters down on the seabed.

e803.text: That day was exactly 100 years since Shackleton's funeral.

e813.text: The ship lay near it, about 10 kilometers away.

e805.text: The team said Worsley's log helped a lot.

e806.text: On the stern, the name ENDURANCE could still be read, letter by letter.

e807.text: Under the name is a five-pointed star, for her original name, Polaris.

e808.text: The Antarctic Treaty protects the wreck from disturbance, so nothing was brought up.

e814.text: To this day no original has been found; it's widely seen as legend.

e810.text: We think what holds this story up isn't the ad but the diaries and logs they wrote themselves.

e811.text: So when someone next quotes that ad, tell them: the ad is lost, but the records remain.

e901.text: Would you take the boat, or wait on the island? Tell me below.

e902.text: This channel only covers what the records hold. Subscribe to open the files with me.
